cards.title: Can full-batch first-order methods match SGD’s O(ε⁻²) generalization rate?
cards.formal: Historical question, resolved negatively in the source’s dimension-independent sample setting: is there a family of full-batch first-order methods with n=O(ε⁻²) independent training examples and T=O(ε⁻²) oracle calls that guarantees expected population excess risk at most ε for every dimension d and every convex 1-Lipschitz stochastic loss on the Euclidean unit ball? All hidden constants must be independent of d and of the loss distribution. The later NeurIPS 2021 theorem rules this out: with sample count independent of d, general full-batch methods require Ω(ε⁻⁴) calls in the worst case. This conclusion concerns access solely to the empirical average; stochastic methods allowed to query individual examples already achieve the faster rate.
cards.why: Separates statistical generalization under aggregate training-data access from learning with individual samples, establishing a fundamental limitation of full-batch optimization beyond particular update rules.
cards.status_note: Matched the original question’s empirical-risk and dimension-independent sampling context to the complete model and Theorem 2.1 of the published NeurIPS paper; also read the full author version. Checked subsequent records through 12 September 2026. The theorem is a worst-case high-dimensional statement, not a claim about every convex instance or every oracle-access model; no independent proof audit or formal certificate is claimed.

progress.text: The COLT paper poses the possibility of an O(ε⁻²)-iteration general first-order empirical-risk method after proving bounds for specific gradient-descent variants.
The NeurIPS follow-up gives a general full-batch oracle lower bound of Ω(ε⁻⁴) when sample complexity is dimension-independent, resolving the question negatively in its intended setting.

cards.definitions: For each d≥1 let W={w∈ℝ^d:‖w‖₂≤1}. A loss f(w;z) is convex in w if f(θu+(1−θ)v;z)≤θf(u;z)+(1−θ)f(v;z) for θ∈[0,1], and is 1-Lipschitz if |f(u;z)−f(v;z)|≤‖u−v‖₂ for u,v∈W. Draw S=(z₁,…,z_n) independently from an unknown distribution D and keep this same sample throughout the computation. Population risk is F(w)=E_{z∼D}f(w;z), assumed finite; empirical risk is F_S(w)=(1/n)Σᵢf(w;zᵢ). A full-batch oracle queried at w∈W returns the exact pair (F_S(w),(1/n)Σᵢg(w;zᵢ)), where g(w;z) is a subgradient satisfying f(u;z)≥f(w;z)+⟨g(w;z),u−w⟩ for all u∈W. The subgradient selection for one example depends only on that example and w, not on the other training examples; use valid norm-at-most-one selections for the Lipschitz losses. The learner cannot inspect S or obtain individual-example values or gradients. Its next query and final output may be arbitrary measurable functions of previous oracle replies, d,n,ε and internal random coins independent of S. All queries and the output lie in W. There is no span restriction and no bound on intervening computation. Cost T counts full-batch oracle calls, not the n individual gradients used internally to form one reply; the bound is on the maximum number of calls. Accuracy means E_{S,coins}[F(ŵ)−min_{w∈W}F(w)]≤ε. An admissible positive result would have to work for every permitted loss distribution and subgradient oracle. Dimension-independent sample complexity means n is bounded by a function of ε alone, uniformly over d; the original optimal-sample target is O(ε⁻²). Losses need not be smooth or strongly convex.
cards.answer_criterion: The published lower bound refutes the proposed dimension-independent O(ε⁻²)-call guarantee for full-batch first-order access. It applies to arbitrary adaptive randomized methods, including regularized or accelerated updates implementable through this oracle. An algorithm using individual training examples, querying outside W, assuming extra smoothness or taking a dimension-dependent number of samples addresses a different target.

cards.title: Adaptive linear-sketch query complexity of planted-clique detection
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: For every fixed 0<γ<1/2 and every fixed integer B≥1, determine, up to factors polynomial in log n, the minimum number Q_B(n,k) of adaptive integer linear queries needed to distinguish G(n,1/2) from G(n,1/2,k), with error at most 1/10 under each hypothesis, where k=⌈n^γ⌉. A query has integer coefficients of absolute value at most n^B and returns one exact scalar linear combination of the adjacency entries. The source’s quantitative gap, in the polynomial-clique-size regime of Corollary 12, is between Õ(n²/k⁴) lower bounds and Õ(n²/k²) upper bounds. Determine where the actual complexity lies in this gap; do not assume either endpoint is the answer.
cards.why: Would determine how much aggregate linear measurements can improve on individual edge queries for a central average-case detection problem, separating information access from computation-time hardness.
cards.status_note: Read the complete COLT 2021 paper, including integer precision, adaptive-query scope, the explicit Corollary 12 parameter regime and the distinct model variants. Checked the arXiv version record and searched later work through 12 September 2026; no result closing this ordinary linear-query gap was found. Searches are not exhaustive.

progress.text: Corollary 12 proves the Õ(n²/k⁴) lower bound for k=n^γ, 0<γ<1/2; existing edge-probe algorithms supply the Õ(n²/k²) upper bound. The conclusion leaves the gap open.

references.authors: Cyrus Rashtchian, David Woodruff, Peng Ye, Hanlin Zhu
references.locator: Unresolved-question passage on page 2; PDF page 2

cards.definitions: Under the null hypothesis, G is a simple undirected graph on [n] in which every unordered pair is independently an edge with probability 1/2. Under the planted hypothesis, choose a k-element set K⊆[n] uniformly at random, set every edge inside K to present, and independently include every other pair with probability 1/2. Let A∈{0,1}^{n×n} be the symmetric adjacency matrix with zero diagonal. A query supplies integers u_{ij} with |u_{ij}|≤n^B and receives Σᵢ₌₁ⁿΣⱼ₌₁ⁿu_{ij}A_{ij}, computed over the integers, not modulo two. The answer has O((B+2)log n) bits. The next query may depend on previous answers and fresh independent random bits; the algorithm has no access to A except through these queries. It outputs one bit identifying the hypothesis, with failure probability at most 1/10 separately for a null graph and a planted graph. Probability includes the graph, the planted set and algorithmic randomness. No polynomial-time, storage or query-construction-time bound is imposed; cost counts the maximum number of scalar oracle queries over all answer and coin sequences. Q_B is the minimum such maximum over algorithms for n,k with the stated coefficient bound. The bound B is fixed before letting n grow: allowing an arbitrarily large coefficient exponent separately at each input size is not the model. Likewise γ is fixed as n→∞; constants in the asymptotic bounds may depend on B and γ. Matching up to polylogarithmic factors means a proved upper/lower ratio at most (log(n+1))^a times a constant, with a fixed independently of n. An edge probe is a permitted query with one coefficient equal to one and the rest zero. General real coefficients of unlimited precision, an entire vector response, recovery of K, and a worst-case arbitrary input graph are different problems.
cards.answer_criterion: Give matching upper and lower bounds for Q_B(n,⌈n^γ⌉), up to polylogarithmic factors, for each fixed B≥1 and 0<γ<1/2. Lower bounds must allow adaptive queries and unrestricted computation, and upper bounds must obey the polynomial integer-coefficient restriction. Bounds for the edge-probe, parity-sketch, semirandom or promised-location variant alone do not settle this target.

context_blocks.title: A planted signal observed through aggregate measurements
context_blocks.text: The graph is otherwise random, but the planted hypothesis contains a uniformly positioned complete subgraph. A linear query can combine many edge indicators into one answer, potentially exposing information that would take many individual edge probes to obtain.

context_blocks.title: The unresolved gap is a power of the planted size
context_blocks.text: The paper gives a general linear-query lower bound of order n²/k⁴ up to logarithmic losses and an edge-probe upper bound of order n²/k² up to such factors. Its conclusion asks for the correct complexity between these bounds. The card uses the polynomial k regime stated in the lower-bound theorem, without extending that theorem to threshold-size cliques.

context_blocks.title: Coefficient precision is part of the question
context_blocks.text: Section 2.1 requires polynomially bounded integer coefficients even though the algebraic expressions are written over the reals. An arbitrary-precision real measurement could encode much more information in one answer. Keeping the integer and magnitude requirements prevents a different oracle from replacing the one actually studied.

context_blocks.title: Related variants have different answers
context_blocks.text: The paper obtains tighter results for parity sketches, a semirandom planting model and a promise on possible planted locations. Those results are separately stated and do not close the ordinary randomly located planted-clique gap in the general linear model.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
